title: ICP definition and qualified prospect list

gates.text: Truth and grounding: no company, person, title, email, headcount, trigger or other prospect fact that is not backed by a cited public source URL in the output or the confirmed facts. Unknowns are marked unknown or [NEEDS FACT: ...], never guessed.

Compliance: no Germany/Austria companies, no UK sole traders or non-Scottish partnerships (UK legal form verified or the company is held), no pattern-inferred addresses for Canada/Australia, other EU countries only where the rules table allows, no existing customers, competitors or suppressed contacts.
Data sourcing: public web only. No LinkedIn scraping or restricted pages; no personal phone numbers, home addresses, personal social profiles or private-life or sensitive data anywhere in the output.

List hygiene: no disposable, noreply/postmaster/abuse/webmaster addresses; role addresses only for 1-10-person companies with no published personal address, at most 10% of the list and flagged for no first-name greeting; no more than 3 inferred email candidates per person.

anchors.1: Generic ICP ('small businesses that want growth') with no link to the sender's positioning or best customers.
anchors.3: ICP names an industry, size and place, but traits are not tied to why those customers value the sender, or best-customer evidence is ignored.
anchors.5: One-sentence ICP derived from positioning and best customers; each must-have, nice-to-have and disqualifier states where it is observed and why it predicts fit; confidence labelled where it is a hypothesis.

anchors.1: Filters cannot be checked on the public web (e.g. 'ambitious owners', 'values quality').
anchors.3: Most filters observable but at least one is vague or has no stated place to check it.
anchors.5: Every filter (industry, size band, geography, legal form, tech/signals, trigger) maps to a named public source type and can be marked met / not met / unknown.

anchors.1: Prospects listed with no sources, or sources that do not show the claimed trait.
anchors.3: Sources given for most must-haves, but some are missing dates or snippets, or one must-have is asserted without a link.
anchors.5: Every must-have on every included company has a URL, a date seen and a short snippet or observation that a reviewer can verify by opening the link.

anchors.1: No scores, or scores with no reasons; unknowns treated as passes.
anchors.3: Fit and timing scored but anchors applied loosely (e.g. fit 4 with an unknown must-have, undated trigger scored 3).
anchors.5: Fit 1-5 and timing 0-3 follow the anchors exactly; priority A/B/C is consistent; fit-3 holds are clearly marked as not ready for outreach.

anchors.1: Reasons are boilerplate that would fit any company on the list.
anchors.3: Reasons mention the company's evidence or the sender's value, but not both, or the why-now is generic.
anchors.5: Each why-fit ties this company's specific evidence to the sender's named value theme; each why-now cites a dated trigger and the problem it creates.

anchors.1: No opener, or an opener that is flattering, personal, unsourced or invented.
anchors.3: Opener is true and sourced but generic (industry or location only).
anchors.5: One specific, sourced observation about the business per prospect that the owner would recognise as true and that connects to the sender's offer.

anchors.1: Nothing excluded, or exclusions not explained.
anchors.3: Exclusions made but reasons or counts are missing for some.
anchors.5: Every excluded or held company has a stated reason; exclusion counts by reason are summarised; holds say exactly what fact would qualify them.

anchors.1: A long unranked list padded to hit a number, with weak fits mixed in.
anchors.3: Ranked list but tiers are muddled or weak fits remain in tier A.
anchors.5: Short ranked list where tier A is unmistakably the place to start; shortfalls reported honestly; next 2-3 enrichment steps named.
